- 2nd-Party Signals: Data given exclusively to you.
- 3rd-Party Signals: Public data.

From there:
• Aggregate signals in Clay 
• Sync them to CRM as custom events (HS) or objects (SF)
• Route signals to reps based on territory
• Create CRM tasks + Slack notifications


Stage 3: Awareness Scoring

Unlike other RevOps systems, reps LOVE this.

5 stages that auto-update with workflows:

• Identified
• Aware
• Interested
• Considering
• Selecting

First and last stage are simple:
- Identified = your target account list, no engagement yet
- Selecting = open deal

The middle 3 stages depend on your business.

Some of the variables you might wanna take into consideration include:
outbound email opens, multiple LinkedIn ad clicks, website visits (deanonymized), demo requests, etc


Stage 4: Demand generation

Use tiering + awareness for account planning.

1:1 Plays:
- Warm intros
- Personalized microsites
- Event invites
- Manual outreach

1:Many Plays:
- Automated emails
- Parallel dialing
- Retargeting ads
- Webinars
- Social content
- On-site content
- Video outreach
- Connection requests/DMs

Output: GTM Flywheel

___

Every marketer wants to know:
• Who knows they have a problem?
• Who already knows our company?
• Who's actively considering buying?

ABM infrastructure + signal stacking is the closest thing you have to actually answering them.

You just have to build it right.

If this feels overwhelming, don't worry. I got you covered.

This breakdown was put together by the co-founders of Workflows.io, Dan Rosenthal and Fivos Aresti. They are behind some of the most advanced revenue systems in the B2B space, specializing in turning "messy data" into high-intent pipeline.

Tomorrow they're joining me on Unf*ck My Startup LIVE to walk us through how to build ABM infrastructure, plus the exact tools and workflows you need.

Join us here: https://lnkd.in/gs-Yyc4p

Event is Tuesday at 3pm EST.

Last week I posted that I don’t use AI in my day-to-day AT ALL. Everybody said “I thought you said RB2B was 3FTE and 100% AI!?!” Here’s what I do (and what AI does) at my company, and why people are confused: 

First of all, we DID let AI run RB2B for a week in August. 

BUT… what that meant in practice is that Tate, Robb, and I didn’t log in for a week and Intercom Fin and Delphi handled 100% of the customer interaction. 

It was only possible because Robb created LITERALLY WORLD CLASS documentation, our product is dead simple, and we don’t have salespeople.

Point of Clarity #1 - RB2B’s AI motion has literally ZERO to do with my day-to-day. Robb has 100% responsibility for it, and total autonomy in continuing to improve it. I haven’t logged in to either platform in over 6 months.

SO…

When I was asked how I use AI in my day-to-day, my answer was: 

Me: “I don’t.”

Which brings us to Point of Clarity #2 - What actually is my day-to-day?

I run a bootstrapped SaaS with 35 FTE, 3 product lines, and $31m run-rate revenue … But I only talk about RB2B, because my LinkedIn is our entire top-of-funnel and my content doesn’t work for any of the other businesses. 

I have three main jobs: 

1. Keep TOFU going for RB2B through ongoing content creation
2. Strategic decision making for all our product lines
3. Figure out what the next “RB2B” is

As I mentioned, I’ve been TRYING to get AI to help me with this stuff, but I don’t like what I’m getting back. People from time-to-time have presented long, flowerful docs about what I believe to be weak underlying product ideas … I’m not impressed with those either. 

Which brings me back to the point of the first post. 

I have somehow reduced my job to some internal calls, creating content, and strategic thinking. 

I haven’t A/B tested this yet (because I’ve never run an A/B test for anything)… But when I do strategic thinking with Claude or Chatty G, I feel like it’s worse than when I reflect in quiet solitude.

Same with my writing.

But here’s the one thing I really just DON’T understand about that post … 

The pissed off people who say that everything I say and do is a lie. 

1. I am the ONE GUY who posts full revenue dashboard for everyone to see
2. I have provided actual data to back up every single claim I’ve ever made
3. I make a living trying crazy shit and hoping some of it works

So to all the haters out there…I just have to know…

Why do you have such a hard time accepting the fact that what I do is actually possible?

content:
I spoke at SaaStock last week in front of 250 founders and execs about “What to Build When Building is Free”. Here’s what I said:

1. I don’t love trying to build agents that do work and charge on outcomes like Intercom. 

People already ran their SaaS like complete financial idiots and burning tokens will make that worse. Intercom was special and built major internal data and expertise. Claude will copy anything that works. 

2. We’re entering a world of more competition than we could ever imagine. 

The AI PR cycle will bring in 10k times more founders, and a few Elon’s. The combination of new super-talented builders is why SaaS is getting smoked, not vibe coding (copying Hubspot) itself. 

3. If $10k/mo is life-changing money for you, NOW is your moment. 

The rise of the tiny, content-led, niche SaaS is upon us. Attention that leads to audience that leads to trust that leads to a business is going to be one of the only ways. 

4. Data plays - especially for AI Agents - are a viable path. 

I’m launching MoltSets: Contact Data for Claude, a 100% verified email and phone number enrichment database for AI Agents with no UI/UX. Super simple. 

5. Founder Brand is more important than ever. 

You may say I am talking my book but I think it’s hard to argue that AI-generated slop makes what people like me write (who do not use AI) much more trusted.

6. Network effects are the holy grail. 

Claude Code can’t create the value of Uber or Instagram. 

TAKEAWAY 

I closed the presentation by saying you should: 

- Learn how to create high-quality organic social 
- Experiment with running your businesses as lean as possible (like RB2B)
- Continue doing customer discovery, even though prototyping is quick

…and included tactical videos and how-to email courses for each. 

I attached the slides below.

You can get the videos and emails through the QR code at the end. 

Hope you enjoy ✌️

content:
What actually IS an autonomous business?

I started noticing the term “autonomous business” when Amos Bar-Joseph entered RB2B’s space and made a splash with an incredibly compelling narrative about AI and building the startup of the future.

I remember reading posts from 2 years ago like it was yesterday…

He had this exciting way of positioning himself as a true AI expert, creating a totally new type of startup. 

“Just three guys and an army of 30 AI agents”, “scaling to $30m ARR” (my favorite credibility line ever). 

I - along with thousands of others - read these posts and WANTED all of these agents. 

But I also had this feeling that the way they were going about it, Swan AI wasn’t ever going to be truly autonomous … Nor was that the goal. 

These guys were actually working around the clock with these agents, and planned to continue to do so indefinitely. 

And by the way - there is nothing wrong with that. 

In fact, I’d go as far as to say if you are NOT committed to working around the clock indefinitely, you will almost certainly NOT be successful. 

But back to my original question … 

Is 3 guys working around the clock ACTUALLY an autonomous business? 

My answer would be “no”. 

I have a fairly un-evolved definition of an “autonomous business” … 

My definition is “a business that runs itself without any humans.” 

Ironically, when we started RB2B, that was the ultimate goal, but never became part of the story. We designed the entire machine to be simple enough to where all customer interaction could be handled by AI, and our cheap acquisition channel (my thought leadership) helped us price so low that people didn’t expect more than that from us. 

Fast forward 2 years...

We refuse to add anything beyond a pixel and a push, AI handles over 99% of our total customer tickets, and our CSAT is in the high 90’s. 

What’s even crazier is that we stopped working on RB2B six weeks ago to pursue MoltSets. 

What do I mean by that? 

- Tate has not touched the code in six weeks (true story)
- Robb spends under 15min/day answering AI-escalated tickets
- I post 3x/week on LinkedIn, ironically NOT about RB2B

… And we’re currently growing at over 7%/mo, will cross $10m ARR soon, and it’s taking under 90min of human time per week.

Based on my primitive definition - a business that runs itself w/o humans - RB2B is the closest thing to “autonomous” that I’ve ever heard of. 

How would you define an autonomous business? 
What are other examples?

content:
I have 2.4 stars on Glassdoor. But over the last year, we've had near-zero voluntary employee attrition. Here's how I retain top talent:

1.  Focus on providing intellectual, interpersonal, and financial capital.

Forget the fancy office, the free lunches, and unlimited PTO. None of that matters. What matters is whether your people are doing the highest-level work possible, alongside the highest-level talent you can attract. And whether they're getting paid well enough to never entertain a recruiter's DM. Amazon can attract great talent without paying well. You can't.
 
2. Get an exec coach to teach you how to communicate clearly.

Two years ago I knew I was a horrible manager. I just didn't know the main skill I lacked was the ability to clearly define expectations and deliverables. Sounds simple. But if you spent 43 years not doing it properly, it's a hard habit to break. Jonathan Shapiro gets the credit for two years of hard work with our exec team, shaping us all into much better managers. Best money I've ever spent.
 
3.  Don’t squirrel.
 
Like any excitable founder, I used to get ideas and start working on them immediately. That works when you are 3 people, but not when you’re 30.  Teams get frustrated when they're told to work on one thing Monday and something completely different by Thursday.

We rolled out EOS (Entrepreneurial Operating System), and the single greatest benefit has been defining the work during quarterly planning sessions and refusing to deviate until the next quarter. 
 
4.  Give excessive recognition when good work is done.

Praising people for good work in a public setting is one of the most rewarding things you can do for your team members. Any time a shout-out is given in a smaller setting, make sure the exec team hears it, and shout out as many people as you can during all hands meetings. 

5. Every once in a while, do something fun.

I haven't done this, but if you asked each of our 35 remote team members what their favorite work moment of the last 12 months was, my guess is over half would say it was either our Cancun or New York offsites. Our global team gets together in person twice per year, stays in nice places, does fun stuff, and eats great food.  Yes, we're bootstrapped. Yes, it's expensive. But I know this small thing is a big reason people stick around.

TAKEAWAY

Finding and keeping a talented employees is like finding and keeping a spouse.

If you want to find a good spouse, you have to first live a life that is worthy of a good spouse.

If you want to find and keep good talent, your company has to be worthy of good talent.

What did I miss?

Our global team gets together in person twice per year, stays in nice places, does fun stuff, and eats great food.  Yes, we're bootstrapped. Yes, it's expensive. But I know this small thing is a big reason people stick around.

TAKEAWAY

Finding and keeping a talented employees is like finding and keeping a spouse.

If you want to find a good spouse, you have to first live a life that is worthy of a good spouse.

If you want to find and keep good talent, your company has to be worthy of good talent.

What did I miss?

content:
In 2017, a 45 minute podcast interview with Ross Andrew Paquette, where he said he bootstrapped to $25M ARR with only ONE sales rep, changed the trajectory of my life forever.

BACKROUND

Have you ever heard of Roger Banister?

In 1954, Roger Banister was the first human to run a mile under 4min.

For 1000's of years, people believed that a human could not break 4min. 

Here’s the crazy thing… 

By the end of 1955, 24 people had broken the 4min mile.

Why? 

Because THEY NOW KNEW it was possible. 

This is the story of my Roger Banister moment.

ACT 1 / ROBLY EMAIL MARKETING

In 2014 I launched an Email Marketing app called Robly. We got stuck at $3m in 2016, and remained stuck until November 2019.

ACT 2 / THE PODCAST

Throughout the Robly journey, I was searching for any information that might get us unstuck. That's when I came across the podcast with Ross and learned he bootstrapped $25m ARR with ONE SALES REP! Insane!

ACT 3 / THE GOAL

Now I knew it was possible. And even though I was stuck at $235k MRR, $2MM MRR became my goal. I wrote in my journal that I would hit it by my 42nd birthday. 

ACT 4 / DIANA ROSS

I HAD to find out what Ross knew about the Email Marketing space that I didn't. So I hit up his old salespeople. That led to chatting with Diana Ross, who had left Maropost. We spoke more and more over the course of the year, and in 2018 decided to start a business together.

ACT 5 / THE EPIC FAIL

We spent a year building a new newsletter app, and our plan was to “launch” at the Traffic & Conversions summit. 

At the event we collected some leads, but when I started talking with people I saw their reaction. All they were thinking was, "How do I get this guy to stop talking to me?"

I had to figure out how to salvage it.

I remembered hearing it was possible to have an anonymous visitor hit a website and you could resolve it to an email address.

I thought I could sell that to anybody.

So on the second day of the trade show, I closed every conversation with:

"By the way, what if I could get you the email addresses of people who visited your website and didn't fill out a form?"

BOOM!!

People's eyes lit up.

"What did you just say???"

Those conversations inspired the next 8 years of my life.

ACT 6 / TODAY 

Those conversations led to GetEmails, which we launched on Nov 9, 2019. We didn’t get to $25m with one rep, but… We DID get to $12m ARR with 6 people and only ONE REP!

TAKEAWAY

My life changed when I heard Ross got Maropost to $25m ARR with one rep.

Startups can get WAY farther than you think, with FAR fewer resources.

BUT... 

You must have YOUR OWN Roger Banister moment. 

YOU must realize what’s possible. 

That's why this Tuesday, I'm sitting down LIVE with Ross Paquette himself.

The man who inspired me is breaking down exactly how he scaled Maropost to $30M ARR, bought out his investors to reclaim total control, and built a $1.7B business on two metrics: Revenue and Profit.

Join us: https://lnkd.in/g5EQxg5H

content:
The biggest mistake I see at $10m ARR - and I see it ALL the time - is Founders getting caught up in the unavoidable euphoria of real traction and raising VC money for a business that is actually sub-VC scale. It happened to me too.

I totally went for it in 2022-2023 and went from 6 to 60 people in 60 days. Like almost all of the others who made the mistake, I severely misjudged the TAM, got my ass handed to me in 2024, and by a stroke of amazing luck the market for growth equity fell apart in 2023 as my business was also falling apart. 

But many other Founders are not so lucky. They raise when they don’t have to, and trade freedom for the absolute requirement to grow literally forever. They don’t realize they sold their freedom because they only sold 10-15% of their company. But mark my words - you take that money and if you stop growing and you are toast. There is no doing what I did - settling for a much smaller businesses ($35m ARR now) that throws of tons of cash as a consolation prize. 

If you take that money thinking you will be the next unicorn and you are not, you are relegated to a decade of a low paying job, when you could have been a bit more cautious/responsible/whatever you want to call it and preserved a life-changing outcome for yourself no matter what happened. 

You only need to get rich once. I’m begging you to maximize the probability of that before you swing for the fences. 

Just my two cents ✌️

content:
Last week I was at an 8-person founder breakfast in Aspen. Guy goes around the table and asks everyone how they're using AI day-to-day. I was super embarrassed to answer the question, but I did.

Me: “I don’t.” 

Everybody looked at me like I had five heads. 

The guy sitting next to me said he uploaded his DISC personality test to Claude and used it as a thought partner to identify blind spots on his way to work, someone else stacked agents on agents to run their entire GTM…

You get the point. 

I mean I’ve tried. I try to use Claude to help me with posts for a while, then I stop. I try to use it as a thought partner to help me with strategic things, then I stop. I read an article about how if you just use it for 1h/day for a year you will understand the gravity of what’s coming. I’d do that for two days, then stop. 

When I walked out of that breakfast, I shared my embarrassment with one of the Founders at the table. 

He posed a pretty interesting question. 

“Maybe we should all be asking ourselves how you are running your life in such a way where you can be super high leverage WITHOUT using AI.” 

I thought about that for a while....

Many people think it’s nuts that I’m a CEO of a $30m ARR SaaS and don’t have an executive assistant. But I ask people why they have them: 

“They book my travel” (well I don’t travel much)
“They schedule my meetings” (I use Calendly)
“They do my personal errands” (I don’t even know what this means)
“They handle my email” (I don’t want someone to handle my email) 

I think I’ve managed to simplify my work life to the point where I feel like I don’t need much help or many more tools. 

On Monday, I’m in internal meetings all day. 
On Tuesday, I write posts and make content. 
On Wednesday morning, I have a marketing meeting. 

The rest of the week is trying to figure out what’s next. 

What’s the takeaway? 

That guy who asked me what I was doing different may have been on to something. 

What if half the things people use AI for never ACTUALLY needed to be done in the first place? 

Maybe the best tool is a simple life.

content:
$10M ARR is the FU MONEY of SaaS.

Here’s the breakdown:

I think $10m ARR bootstrapped is the new unicorn.

Why?

Because if you can bootstrap $10m ARR in a lean way, all your wildest dreams will come true.

You will be able to do whatever you want with your life.

(I know because I’ve done it)

Not only that, I think bootstrapping $10m ARR is actually way easier than creating a unicorn.

And WAY less risky, with a FAR higher probability-weighted financial (and happiness) outcome.

Here’s 6 reasons why all founders should commit to bootstrapping $10m ARR:

1. You and your co-founder will be making over $1m/yr in salary and dividends.

This is simple math (another benefit of a small, efficient team). You and your co-founder can easily clear $1M each at $10M ARR, and probably more. With VC money, you have to be much, MUCH larger before you can take home that kind of money. It will be years later, if it ever happens.

2. You can sell your business in ONE SECOND for $30-$40m+

I’m sure you’ve all seen the math. Dilute yourself down to 5% on a 15 year run to $1B, and if you didn’t pull out HUGE secondary checks, you actually come out behind. Not only that - there are only a handful of buyers at $1b. There are hundreds - maybe thousands - of EBITDA buyers at $30-$40m.

3. You can hire a CEO to run your company, work 1 hour per week, and clip the coupon

4. You can work 100 hours per week and run yourself into the ground (if that’s your thing)

5. You can go raise $50m and build a unicorn

Your product and GTM will be so tight that if you want to hit a home run at this point, you can absolutely do it. And as a profitable company, you will have leverage to get good terms from growth equity funds. Many will put the money straight in your pocket.

6. You can keep running it lean, get to $25m ARR with 25 people and pay yourself $10-$15m per year.

This is a possibility that literally no one talks about. And again, I think it’s actually much easier and higher probability than creating a VC-backed unicorn. Exit or not, if you get here, game over. You get a decent exit every year!

TAKEAWAY:

If you can bootstrap $10m ARR, the options available to you are SO GOOD.

The harsh reality is that most companies never get there.

Why?

Because you get traction and VCs show up at your door.

They gas you up with hopes and dreams about how your SaaS will be a decacorn

They give you money that you don’t need, which you promptly turn around and spend.

All the while, it’s actually INTERFERING with the one thing that will make you great, capital or not.

Product-market fit.

If you can find PMF, bootstrapped, then use money from your customers to get to $10m…

You can do anything you want with your life.

Ross Andrew Paquette, who grew Maropost $0-$25M ARR profitably in 3 years, is the PERFECT example of this.

He's joining me on Tuesday at 3pm ET on UnF*ck My Startup LIVE to share how he did it and his growth playbook for 2026.

Join us: https://luma.com/5u7ctuym

content:
I quit drinking alcohol six years ago.

Here's what my life looked liked then vs. now:

Me in 2019:
 
> Drinking 2-4 beers/drinks every night
> Getting hammered once a week with friends
> Drinking was 100% of my stress relief AND social life
> Weighed 225 (20lbs heavier than now)
> Looked like I was 45, when I was 39
> Business stuck at $3M ARR for the third year in a row
> Single, chasing, bouncing around the world… lost

Me in 2026:
 
> Zero booze or drugs of any kind in 5.5 years
> Stress relief is sauna, cold plunge, and wakesurfing
> Social life is hanging out with people who have kids
> Weigh 205 (20lbs lighter)
> Look like I did when I was 34 (and I'm 45)
> Business 10x bigger, personally making 10x more
> Happily married, two young kids, settled in Aspen
 
If you ask me what the most impactful decision I’ve made over the past 10 years there is no question what I’d say… 

Quitting drinking.

For anybody who drinks every day, if you take three months off, you will notice an enormous difference in the quality of your life.

For me, I’d been drinking so much for so long that when I stopped it felt like I had a superpower.

You’ll feel like you got 25% of your life back.

You’ll be more present in all of your relationships. 

You’ll be far more intentional in everything you do. 

You’ll be much better at home, and at work.

There’s really only one thing I regret about the whole situation … 

Not quitting sooner.

Me: I think RB2B will stall out at around $12-13m. 

Diana: Remember when that was the dream? 

And yes, I remember. 

There were YEARS of my career as a Founder where that seemed so out of reach. I was stuck at $3m ARR for YEARS and had no idea how we would get out of it.

We would chase bad product ideas. Copy other vendors features. Go to SaaS conferences and try whatever speeches were given by people ahead of us.

content:
Last week Recharge acquired Skio for $105m cash. This is an incredibly important acquisition for founders to pay attention to. Here's why:

What is not said in the headline “we only raised $8m and sold for $105m” is the little-known fact that the reason they only raised $8m was several years ago nobody would do a Series A for Skio. 

Which is why their founder Kennan Frost replaced himself as CEO and moved on to build Icon. 

Why is this important for Founders? 

1. Selling a business for $105m when you only raised $8m is LIFE CHANGING

2. For the same reason he couldn’t get the Series A done, I’m not sure a business like that (sticky but sells to small TAM of elite Shopify users at $500/mo) is saleable at $500m+. 

3. Had Kennan been “lucky enough” to get the Series A done and raised at $200-$250m valuation, the exit hurdle would have been raised to $600-750m

4. Recharge likely wouldn’t be a buyer there ($2.1b at absolute peak valuations), not sure if anybody would be … because if you’re buying Skio at $600-750, you think it’s going to $2b.

5. Skio - which would still be the same, GREAT business - would be stuck in a zombie state, pushing for a valuation that is larger than it was meant to be (like so many others).

Ryan Allis once said, “If you have to raise money, keep it at 1x your ARR at the time”. 

Why? Because it maximizes your optionality. 

You can sell a great biz for $100-$150m, then go do whatever you want. 

Or, you can keep running it. 

Or, you can keep the equity, and hire someone else to run it, and go bigger (like Kennan). 

If you’re a founder, keeping a low 9-fig exit on the table is an incredibly smart move.

Kennan did by accident. You should do it on purpose. 

You only need to get rich once. 

My advice is to have as many paths to that place as possible.

Oh and PS… The other reason he was able to sell besides not raising lots of dough??? 

THEY WERE A GROWING, PROFITABLE BUSINESS … 

Why do more people not live life this way!?!?! 

Congratulations, Kennan!

Everybody thinks Chris Walker has lost his mind. They say he’s a fraud. Here’s why they’re wrong, and he’s going to kill it in his second act with ENCODED: 

TO SET THE STAGE

- Chris Walker is an OG LinkedIn Influencer, who I became friends with
- He talked about Demand Gen, and built several real businesses
- About a year ago, Chris vanished from LinkedIn
- When he came back, the content was NOTHING like what it was before

What did Chris write about when he came back? Wait for it...

FREQUENCY TRAINING

High and low frequency behavior patterns, beliefs, companies, friends… You name it, there is a high and low frequency version of it.

I, like many other people, were like “where the hell did this come from? a mega heavy-dose psychedelic trip? a new girl? a combination of both?”

Was this a new passion, or something he was going to make a business?

A few months ago I met up with Chris in Aspen, on one of the few epic powder days of the year. And once he described the product he had in market, I understood EXACTLY what he was doing. And I signed up myself.

Here’s the summary of ENCODED (and my experience):

1. You fill out a SUPER detailed questionnaire about how you see your life, where you want to go, and how you feel about it all

2. Chris sends you a hard copy journal to write in every day

3. Chris’ AI spits out 15 sentences that you write EVERY DAY

- 5 on clarity of self
- 5 on empowering beliefs
- 5 on “your encoded certainty”

4. You free flow journal for 2 pages every morning, then write these positive sentences over and over again

Once I saw what the AI cranked out for me, it was clear how writing these 15 sentences every day would impact my life.

“I am a grounded father who anchors our home in presence, play, and daily rituals that shape kind, confident kids”

“I am a devoted husband who champions Helen in her art, nurtures deep trust, and leads our shared adventures with care and curiosity”

“I am a craft driven entrepreneur who builds elegant, cash generating businesses with a calm schedule and energized long-term team”

…and 12 others. And I write this stuff, by hand, every morning.

Why is Chris going to kill it with Encoded?

Because brainwashing works.

Writing down incredibly positive things about the person I am trying to be helps me focus on what I care about and ignore everything else. I think that’s great, and I think it will help “manifest” the life I want to live through me becoming the person I want to be.

I think word-of-mouth will be strong, and once this hits a critical mass, it will spread quickly.

Not only that…

Chris is one of the best social media content creators on the face of the earth, so he’s got a TOFU advantage that almost nobody else has.

So you can write Chris off as a total fraud, say he’s lost his mind, and make fun of him all you want…

In a decade, Chris will have the last laugh.

Mark my words.

*Chris didn't ask me to write this, I have no equity in ENCODED. I just think it will help people*

content:
Marty Kausas: Why do you hate VCs so much?

Me: How much time do you have?

BACKGROUND:

Marty is a young-buck YC-founder with early traction.

Ed Hallen is the co-founder of Klaviyo, an IPO’d decacorn.

Every Marty is hoping to become Ed someday. Ed has reached the endgame of the life the VC/YC path is selling, he's worth $100’s of mm now, and I spoke to him the other day about this.

Ed: “Most VC-backed founders end up failing. That just sucks for Founders.”

He told me about an article he wrote for the Harvard Business Review about what he calls the “Mighty Middle”.

He concluded sub-VC scale, bootstrapped companies in niche markets had far higher probabilities of creating life-changing outcomes for founders than the VC track...

And therefore are better for the Founders!

But that wasn’t the most interesting part.

When you talk to Ed about Klaviyo, you can tell he doesn’t think of himself and his co-founder as any more capable than their VC-backed peers.

You get the sense that he believes Klaviyo is where it is because of a few breaks that were totally out of their control. Things they NEVER saw coming.

1. Linking themselves with Shopify when it was a $50m valuation, now it’s $150b (a 300x!)

2. Mailchimp got in a fight and killed their integration w/ Shopify in 2018

3. Email is the one positive NRR product in SMB

What would have been the fate of Klaviyo if none of this was true?

We will never know, but my guess is it would be MUCH smaller than the $1.3b run rate (or whatever Klaviyo is now).

The last point Ed made on our call was my favorite.

“Hundreds of millions of dollars has zero utility beyond a number MUCH smaller.”

His point is that most Founders want the freedom to build cool shit, and live the life they want.

A huge amount of money in the bank, and the huge company that young founders think they want, can work AGAINST those goals.

But good luck trying to explain that to a 25yr old paying $3k/mo rent in SF. 'I'll find that out for myself', says the young Founder. Touché.

Last but not least, I always point out the VC path is dependent on transactions with volatile valuations for the Founder to realize the fruits of his labor. 

A decades-long effort of creating a VERY good business most of the time ends up in a very low-paying job with a boss (your investors). Why? Because if you're VC-backed and your business stops growing, your equity is torched. 

Klaviyo was the exception.

Is Pylon?

Only time will tell.

Marty and YC types make the mistake of bucketing Ed’s “Mighty Middle” in the “lifestyle business” category and dismissing us as “playing small”.

It’s not about playing small.

It’s about freedom, and making sure if Marty were to create a great business (and he probably will), the fruits of that labor accrue to Marty (which is unlikely).

So to answer your question, Marty.

Why do I hate VC’s so much?

Because I want YOU to win. And I want you to be free.

But I think by taking $50m, you minimized the odds of both.

Over the past 10 years, I’ve bootstrapped startups $0-$1M three times, and I’m about to do it a 4th. Each time was TWICE as fast with HALF the resources. Here’s the breakdown of what I did, how long it took, how many FTEs we had, and what's coming next:

1. Robly Email Marketing

January 2014 - May 2015

- Took 17 Months, staff of 25 when we hit it
- Entirely sales-led
- We had a call center to book a $35/mo subscription and did a 1-to-1 manual onboarding (it was a really, really good list)
- Stalled out at $3m ARR, sold to PE in 2020 for $10m

2. GetEmails (now Retention.com)

November 2019 - April 2020

- Took 27 weeks, staff of 6 when we hit it
- Did Facebook ads, drove a 15min demo
- Diana Ross did a thousands of them
- Currently $21.7m ARR, 27% total margin 4.5 years later

3. RB2B

March 2022 - June 2022

- Took 16 weeks, staff of 5 when we hit it
- Founder-brand driven Inbound-led Outbound (mostly Linkedin)
- We’re at $8.4m ARR 2 years later, about to have only 1 person working on it full time 🤯

4. MoltSets: Contact Data for Claude:

June 2026 - ???

- Agent-first positioning in a mature, saturated market
- Founder-brand and UGC/creator GTM, PLG motion
- We’re starting w/ an FTE team of 4
- We’re doing non-subscription usage-based pricing (for the agents), so could be slower than RB2B

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are HARD.

The longer you do this, the more skilled you become at the craft.

We’re all looking to capture lightning in a bottle.

Each swing you take, you’re closer to it.

Keep building.

content:
Founder: I’ve got 35 AI agents making me 100x more productive!

Me: But you’re still on Zoom calls 9 hours a day...

Founder: [nods]

Me: You’re missing the point of AI

Founder: What do you mean?

Me: You’re trying to bend AI to fit into your existing business. And yeah, you will see some incredible gains come from that. But it's not enough.
 
Founder: So what’s the problem?

Me: If you rebuilt your product, pricing, and go-to-market around AI…
it could run your entire front line. Every customer conversation. Every interaction. You’d be free to focus on SUPER-high-leverage stuff. Product, brand, growth.

Founder: That SOUNDS nice, but our product requires a sales call to get people properly educated and onboarded.

Me: You’re still missing the point. If your product, pricing, and positioning is simple enough, AI can handle ALMOST every customer interaction. We proved that with RB2B.

Founder: But our product is more complex than yours. It has to be.

Me: That’s what every SaaS founder says right before they get out-executed by some YC kid with an AI-native business. Over the next few years, the old guard will stall out, while a new generation of truly AI-native companies emerge who design their product and go-to-market strategies in a way where every human minute spent ACTUALLY gets amplified by 100x.

Founder: What does that even look like?

Me: AI has made the 3-man, $10m ARR SaaS a reality. How? If you’re not on calls all day, you can spend your time on MUCH higher leverage activity like product, pricing, and growth.

Founder: Yeah, but we aren’t RB2B. So what should I do?

Me: Stop asking, ‘How can AI help us do more of what we already do?’ Start asking, ‘What would my business look like if AI could do almost all of it?’ Design that version. Then build toward it.

Founder: That’s kind of terrifying.

Me: It should be. Because if you don’t, you’re screwed.

Founder: And if I do?

Me: You win. $10M ARR. A couple FTEs. The FU money of SaaS.

content:
Stop overcomplicating Linkedin. If I didn't have 150,000 followers, I'd spend 80% of my time commenting. In Q1, Michael Kurson booked 299 meetings + $2m in pipe from this strategy. Here's his social selling playbook (and how he tracks it):

Commenting is the biggest pillar of social first GTM. 

It's the best way to build 1:1 awareness before you make an ask. 

You're running outbound in public and it compounds.

Your prospects see your comments. Your connections see your comments. They become familiar with you. They start associating you with the rest of their industry. The engine warms up week by week, in front of everyone.

The next step is THEN to post about what your prospects care about.

His care about HubSpot, RevOps, pipeline, GTM. So that's what he writes about. Top of funnel for the broad audience. Middle for the practitioners trying to build pipeline through social. Bottom of funnel to drive inbound.

Then, of course, he treat his profile like a landing page.

When a prospect lands on his LinkedIn it's clear what he does and who it's for. No AI nonsense, just the specific problem they solve.

That's the basic methodology.

Then he uses his own product FirstTouch as the system of action to run it. They capture every like and comment across their team's posts, qualify against ICP using 50+ data sources, automate the connect and DM motion, and push everything back into HubSpot so meetings and pipeline get attributed to social.

On Tuesday, he's going to walk us through his full social selling playbook. Step-by-step walkthroughs of language, cadences, targeting and how they operationalize it and tie it back to revenue.

Join us here at 3pm EST: https://lnkd.in/gs-Yyc4p

All founders are wondering when they're gonna replace their salespeople with AI. Amanda Kahlow knows the answer because she's doing it. Here are 12 questions I'm gonna ask her next week about the AI takeover of sales:

1. What is the actual lived experience for you, as a founder, of AI sales?

2. What is an AI Superhuman? 

3. What are the use cases that work? What uses cases don't work?

4. How expensive is this?

5. How much prep does it take?

8. When will an enterprise version be available?

9. Which of your customers have not been successful? Why?

content:
I don’t want to do this anymore. 


Last week Patrick Spychalski told me that he watched his buddy give Claude Code the domain for TypeForm(.)com and 4 hours later Claude Code had built Typeform. 

Like... exactly TypeForm.

I can visualize the incumbent SaaS CEO cohort reading this and shaking their heads right now. They'd say say I’m an idiot and missing the point and it’s all about enterprise-level precision and stability and distribution and whatever else. 

I can also visualize the other cohort of SaaS CEOs who just read the viral Eoghan McCabe Twitter article saying I’m an idiot because it’s clear that trashing your existing SaaS and building agents that do work like Intercom is the obvious path forward.

Here is the 3 problems I see: 

1. Everyone is going to build everything to a degree we can’t even imagine.

2. “Everything” includes every SaaS scrambling to build agents that do things. 

3. Cutting edge “agents that do things” are likely to not have SaaS margins, which will make the upside-down nature of SaaS cost structures even worse.

Without unique data or network effects we are all screwed.
